name: Testosterone replacement therapy

lead: Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) is medical supplementation of testosterone to restore normal levels in people with hypogonadism. In appearance circles it is noted for its virilizing effects, including more muscle and a deeper voice.

Exogenous testosterone restores androgen receptor signalling and suppresses the body's own production through the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. In hypogonadal men, trials have reported gains in fat-free mass, muscle size and metabolic markers. Testosterone can deepen the voice in people such as women or transgender men receiving it, though voice is not a studied TRT goal.

paras: It is prescribed after diagnosis and monitored with blood tests, in injection, gel, patch, pellet or oral forms. Muscle and body-composition changes in trials develop over months and are generally paired with resistance training.

Reported risks include raised hematocrit, sleep apnea, fertility suppression, acne, prostate concerns and cardiovascular questions, which the 2023 TRAVERSE trial studied; FDA warning language was revised in 2025. It requires diagnosis and monitoring and is a controlled substance in many countries.

web.title: T Nation: Actors, Athletes, and Influencers on Steroids

angle.text: Medical testosterone restores normal levels in hypogonadism, and its androgen effects add muscle and can deepen the voice. Trials in hypogonadal men have studied muscle and metabolic outcomes; voice is not a studied purpose.

lead: Testosterone replacement therapy (TRT), also called androgen replacement therapy, is the medical use of testosterone to bring hormone levels back to the normal range in people with hypogonadism, mainly men. It can be given by injection, gel, patch, pellet or other routes, and is a controlled prescription drug in most countries.[1][2]

For appearance, TRT works through the hormone's normal roles in muscle, fat, skin, hair and the voice. In men with low testosterone, trials report gains in fat-free mass and muscle size, and testosterone also affects oiliness of skin, acne and scalp hair; in transgender men it is used for its virilizing effects such as voice deepening, facial and body hair and a more masculine fat distribution.[3][2] In lifting communities, men on TRT are often described as leaner and more muscular year-round, and some commentators there call it a form of mild steroid use.[4]

Research concentrates on safety and symptom relief. The 2023 TRAVERSE trial of more than 5,000 men found testosterone non-inferior to placebo for major cardiovascular events, and the FDA revised the boxed warning in 2025.[5][2] Effects include raised hematocrit, suppressed sperm production, acne, possible worsening of sleep apnea and, in some people, hair loss.[2][6]
infobox: Intramuscular or subcutaneous injection, transdermal gel or patch, subdermal pellet, buccal, oral and nasal forms[2]
Cypionate, enanthate, propionate, undecanoate, mixed esters[2]
AndroGel, Aveed, Testopel, Sustanon and others[2]
US Schedule III; Canada Schedule IV; UK Class C; Rx-only in EU; banned by WADA[2]

paras: The main indication is male hypogonadism, defined as persistently low serum testosterone together with symptoms such as low libido, fatigue, reduced muscle mass or low mood.[6][1] It is used in primary hypogonadism (testicular failure) and secondary hypogonadism (hypothalamic or pituitary causes), and to induce and maintain secondary sex characteristics.[1][6] A 2020 American College of Physicians guideline supports discussing it for age-related low levels in men with sexual dysfunction, with annual reassessment.[2] In 2015 the FDA stated that benefits and safety for age-related decline had not been established.[2]

Testosterone is also given to transgender men for virilization, titrated to typical male levels, and short-term use has been studied for low sexual desire in postmenopausal women, although no testosterone product is approved for women in the US.[2]

Testosterone promotes muscle growth and maintenance and influences fat distribution, skin oiliness, body and facial hair, and voice pitch.[2] That is why TRT is discussed in physique communities as well as in clinics. A T Nation article describes TRT as a form of mild steroid use and says men on it tend to look lean and muscular all year, while a reply in the same thread objects that testosterone does not automatically produce the extreme behaviours attributed to it.[4]
Many men also report that restoring testosterone lifts energy and mood, which supports training consistency; trials of mood effects are covered under clinical studies.

A 1997 study in hypogonadal men reported that testosterone replacement increased fat-free mass and muscle size.[3] Reviews of the field say replacement may improve sexual function, depressive symptoms, bone density and lean body mass, while evidence on cardiovascular events and mortality had been conflicting before TRAVERSE.[6][7]

Trials in hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes reported effects on insulin resistance, glycaemic control, visceral adiposity and cholesterol, including the 2006 study in the European Journal of Endocrinology and the TIMES2 study in Diabetes Care.[8][9] A 2024 Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology review notes that in men with functional hypogonadism, large trials and an individual-patient meta-analysis show modest but significant improvements in sexual function and improved bone mineral density and insulin sensitivity, while evidence is insufficient to show fracture or diabetes prevention.[7]

Wikipedia lists acne, oily skin, scalp hair loss, swelling, breast enlargement, mood changes, increased hematocrit and worsened sleep apnea among reported effects, with liver and heart effects described as serious but less common.[2] Testosterone can be converted to estradiol, mainly in fat tissue, and gynecomastia can occur at high doses.[2] 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors may reduce androgenic skin and hair effects but can also blunt body and facial hair growth.[2] Injectable undecanoate can cause pulmonary oil microembolism in under 1 percent of injections per year in Aveed's labeling.[2]

Exogenous testosterone suppresses the body's own production through feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and can reduce sperm production, sometimes reversibly; a 2025 Nature Reviews Urology paper reviews TRT and spermatogenesis in men of reproductive age.[2][10] Clinicians recommend PSA and digital rectal exams before and during therapy, and monitoring of hematocrit and symptoms.[2][11][6]

A 2004 NEJM review set out risks and monitoring recommendations.[11] Earlier concerns came from the halted TOM trial and a 2013 JAMA study, and in 2015 the FDA required heart attack and stroke warnings.[2] TRAVERSE enrolled 5,246 men aged 45 to 80 with symptoms of hypogonadism, low testosterone and existing or high risk of cardiovascular disease, and tested non-inferiority against placebo; the authors and later reviews report no increase in major adverse cardiovascular events.[5][6] In February 2025 the FDA removed cardiovascular language from the boxed warning and added a blood pressure warning.[2]

A JAMA Network Open analysis of TRAVERSE examined prostate events, comparing TRT with placebo for high-grade prostate cancer, any prostate cancer, acute urinary retention and procedures.[12] A depression substudy examined mood responses.[13]

Men naturally produce roughly 3 to 11 mg of testosterone per day, mostly in testicular Leydig cells under control of pituitary luteinising hormone.[2][14] Replacement uses esters that are released slowly after injection or absorbed through skin; the intramuscular route is the most common, and AndroGel is reported as the most popular US gel.[2] The 2020 ACP guideline preferred intramuscular over transdermal routes because effectiveness and harms are similar and injections are cheaper.[2]

Testosterone was isolated in 1935 and approved for medical use in 1939; Grokipedia credits Adolf Butenandt and Leopold Ruzicka, who shared the 1939 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for related work, and describes injection therapy for hypogonadism from the 1940s.[2][1] US use roughly tripled between 2001 and 2011, and testosterone is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[2] The US Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 1990 made testosterone and other anabolic steroids controlled substances.[2]

Testosterone is Schedule III in the US, Schedule IV in Canada and Class C in the UK, and is prescription-only in the EU.[2] The World Anti-Doping Agency lists it as a prohibited anabolic agent, and detection relies on measures such as the testosterone-to-epitestosterone ratio.[2]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and lifting communities
paras: TRT forums on T Nation cover lab interpretation, estradiol and symptoms; threads document users who say they felt better, and others who report little change after years on therapy.[15][16] T Nation author TC Luoma frames clinic TRT as a continuous low-level steroid regimen, a view that sits alongside medical guidance describing it as replacement of a deficiency.[4][6] Voice deepening and other virilizing effects are discussed mainly in connection with transgender men and women.[2]

Randomised trials include TRAVERSE (cardiovascular safety, 5,246 men) and its prostate and depression analyses, the TIMES2 study in men with type 2 diabetes or metabolic syndrome, a double-blind trial in hypogonadal men with type 2 diabetes, and a randomised trial on sexual function and hypogonadal symptoms.[5][12][13][9][8][17] A 1997 trial reported increases in fat-free mass and muscle size.[3]

Registered trials include testosterone in kidney transplantation, prostate cancer active surveillance and hypogonadism, and a 2026 randomised trial in prostate cancer survivors with hypogonadism.[18][19][20] No studies were found of TRT for voice deepening in men.
